# Digest D — Phil 2:6–18 Christ hymn block

**Source:** G. Walter Hansen, *The Letter to the Philippians* (PNTC)  
**Slice:** `slice_D_hymn_2_6-11.txt` (raw lines ~1756–2064)  
**Sections covered:** §2 Christ Hymn: Humility (2:6–8); §3 Christ Hymn: Exaltation (2:9–11); §D Work Out Your Salvation (2:12–18)  
**Extractor note:** Subagent extraction only — no wiki edits. All claims attributed to Hansen’s exposition; debates recorded as positions he reports or takes.

## Hansen’s working renderings of 2:6–11 (vs TNIV) — as they appear in this slice

Hansen does not restate the full six-stanza translation in this slice (that sits in C with Lohmeyer’s layout). In D he works with these characteristic renderings and TNIV comparisons:

| Hansen’s working language in D | TNIV / other cited renderings | Locus |
|---|---|---|
| First stanza = preincarnate **attitude of mind**: “he did not consider his divine form, his equality with God, **an advantage to exploit**” | — | D l. 3 |
| *Harpagmos* preferred: “**an advantage to exploit**” / “something to be selfishly exploited that is already possessed” | KJV “robbery”; RSV/NIV “thing/something to be grasped” | D ll. 75, 91 |
| “**existing** in the form of God” (not “was the form of God”) | TNIV “being in very nature God” — Hansen concludes the hymn **points to** that sense via glory/being union | D ll. 15–17, 53 |
| Kenosis: “**He emptied himself!**”; conclusion fuses three views; TNIV “he **made himself nothing** by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness” | TNIV cited approvingly for kenosis meaning | D ll. 95, 107, 119 |
| “**taking** the form of a slave” / “**becoming** in the likeness of **human beings**” (anthropoi gender-inclusive) | TNIV “human likeness” | D ll. 121–127 |
| “**in appearance being found as a human being**” | — | D ll. 130–133 |
| “**humbled himself**… **by becoming obedient unto death**… **even death on a cross**!” | — | D ll. 135–149 |
| “**Therefore also** God highly exalted him” | TNIV “to the highest place” for *hyperypsōsen* | D ll. 165, 175 |
| Name given = **Lord** (*kyrios*), not the earthly name Jesus | Moule’s view: name given = Jesus — reported and rejected | D ll. 179–187 |
| Purpose: every knee **bow**, every tongue **acknowledge** that **Jesus Christ is Lord**, to the glory of **God the Father** | — | D ll. 189–209 |

## Claims

### A. 2:6–8 — Humility / preexistence / form of God / *harpagmos* / kenosis

**C1. First stanza as preincarnate attitude.**  
Hansen: the first stanza “speaks of Christ’s **preincarnate attitude of mind**: he did not consider his divine form, his equality with God, an advantage to exploit.”  
- Quote: “The first stanza of the hymn speaks of Christ’s preincarnate attitude of mind…”  
- Locus: D l. 3

**C2. “Existing” does not itself prove preexistence; narrative sequence does.**  
Hansen: the participle *existing* “does not in itself denote preexistence”; it “simply points to a state or circumstance of being.” Preincarnate reading comes from **relation** of present participle *existing* to later aorists (*emptied*, *taking*, *becoming*) in one continuous sentence to the cross.  
- Quotes: “This word does not in itself denote preexistence.” / “existing in the form of God comes before the actions described by… he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, and becoming in the likeness of human beings.”  
- Locus: D ll. 5–11  
- Note: Hansen **takes** preincarnate/preexistence reading on narrative-temporal grounds.

**C3. “In the form of God” = sphere/location; clothed in form of God.**  
Hansen: text says Christ was existing **in** the form of God, not that he **was** the form of God; idiomatic parallel Luke 7:25 (clothed in expensive clothes).  
- Quote: “Christ was clothed in the form of God.”  
- Locus: D ll. 13–15

**C4. Lexical *morphē* = outward appearance.**  
Standard lexicon: “outward appearance and shape”; Greek literature and LXX use for what can be seen; works for both “form of God” and “form of a slave.”  
- Locus: D ll. 17–19

**C5. Problem: invisible God and “form.”**  
Hansen notes Jewish impossibility of God having sensual form open to perception (vs Greek gods); OT anthropomorphisms figurative; image prohibition protects transcendence — hence “oxymoron: What is the form of God?”  
- Locus: D ll. 19

**C6. Lightfoot/Aristotle line (reported).**  
Lightfoot: *morphē* ≈ attributes/essential nature of Godhead (Aristotelian form vs matter); “in the form of God” = participation in being/essence of God. Many commentaries influenced.  
- Hansen: helpful but **doubts** legitimacy of restricting *morphē* to Aristotelian technical sense; still finds Lightfoot’s **conclusion** (“true divine nature”) confirmed by another route.  
- Locus: D ll. 19–21

**C7. Hansen’s preferred route: *morphē theou* = glory of God.**  
OT/NT glory as outward manifestation of God’s power/majesty; long Exodus–Ezekiel list; Rom 1:20–23; 2 Cor 4:6.  
- Quotes: “the form of God in which the preincarnate Christ was clothed was the glory of God.” / “existing in the form of God points to Christ’s being in very nature God (TNIV).”  
- Method contrast: same conclusion as Lightfoot but “derived from… biblical connection” of outward appearance (*morphē*) with glory-manifestation, not Aristotle.  
- Conclusion: hymn places preincarnate Christ “in the glory of God” and asserts “intimate union of Christ with the being of God” / “essential equality with God” without offering Aristotelian metaphysics.  
- Locus: D ll. 21–53

**C8. Parallelism: form of God ↔ to be equal with God.**  
Third line of first stanza clarifies first: “to be equal with God” affirms the one in form of God is not less than/different from God; yet two distinguishable persons — later: Jesus worshipped as Lord **to the glory of God the Father**; not a second god; worship of Jesus “inclusion within and extension of the worship of the one God.”  
- Locus: D ll. 55

**C9. Adam/Christ /*eikōn* alternative (reported, qualified).**  
Some equate form of God with image of God → extended Adam/Christ hymn. Dunn: hymn “dominated by the Adam/Christ parallel”; terms lack independent value within Adam Christology.  
- Counter-arguments Hansen relays (Hurtado et al.): *morphē*/*eikōn* not strict equivalents; nowhere is “form of God” used interchangeably with “image of God”; no Genesis wording beyond “God” in the hymn to ground allusion.  
- Hansen: resist building **entire** interpretation on Adam parallel **yet** network of Phil 2 ↔ Gen 1–3 associations supported via Paul’s letters (Rom 5; 1 Cor 15; image/glory of Christ). Expanded equation: form of God — glory of God — image of God (via 2 Cor 3:18; 4:4–6). Paul would hear *morphē theou* as glory allusion and **echo** of image.  
- Locus: D ll. 57–61

**C10. Denial of personal preexistence via Adam parallel (reported and rejected).**  
Dunn: Adam not preexistent → no intended implication of Christ’s preexistence; focus on parallel choices (Adam grasps Gen 3:5; Christ does not). Brown: form of God = earthly life as manifestation of God.  
- Hansen’s rebuttal: narrative collapses if already-human Christ “emptied himself… becoming in likeness of human beings” and “found in appearance as a human being” — redundant unless pre-human existence; repeated human-likeness language hugely significant only if consequence of preincarnate choice.  
- Wright, Caird, Ridderbos (reported affirmatively for Hansen’s side): Adam contrast **requires** preexistence/incarnation reversal; Ridderbos: pre-human divine mode already “second Adam.”  
- Hansen: even before incarnation, as one in form of God, Christ already “divine original” for humanity in God’s image; incarnation/death/exaltation opens way for humanity to share original’s glory (links Phil 3:21).  
- Locus: D ll. 65–69

**C11. *Harpagmos* rare and disputed; four definitions Hansen treats.**  
Word nowhere else in NT/LXX; rare in Greek literature. Preferred translation: “**an advantage to exploit**.” Four options:  
1. **Active grasping for something already possessed** (KJV “robbery”): equality not by robbery but inherent right. Objection: context stresses renunciation not claim of rights. Variant: precisely **because** in form of God, equality = giving not getting (causative not concessive participle) — God’s essence self-giving. Object-lack debate (Foerster vs Wright).  
2. **Passive: prize already possessed, not clutched** (RSV/NIV “something to be grasped”): Lightfoot paraphrase — did not treat equality as prize greedily clutched; resigned “glories of heaven,” not divinity itself. Barth: renounce outward appearance/credit without surrendering being.  
3. **Something not possessed, not to be grasped** (Adam-Christ): Dunn — refusal to grasp equality as Adam did, throughout life/ministry. Martin mediating: possessed divinity (*morphē*) but not equality (= cosmic Lordship) until after humiliation — Hansen **rejects** as conflicting grammar (articular infinitive points back to form of God = same reality) and theology (exaltation affirms incarnation/death as revelation of divine love, not acquisition of equality previously lacking).  
4. **Something already possessed, not to be selfishly exploited** (Hoover idiom): Hansen’s preferred line. Equality = divine nature/position preincarnate; decision not to exploit for selfish advantage **expresses** equality; “uniquely qualifying him” for redemptive suffering.  
- Quotes: “The pre-existent son regarded equality with God not as excusing him from the task of (redemptive) suffering and death, but actually as uniquely qualifying him for that vocation.” / Divine “No” to exploitation vs Philippi’s emperors/gods (Caligula, Nero, Alexander, Apollo, Zeus).  
- Locus: D ll. 73–93  
- **Hansen’s position:** reading (4); equality possessed and expressed, not discarded or newly acquired at exaltation.

**C12. Kenosis: three interpretations; Hansen combines elements.**  
Shocking metaphor: “He emptied himself!” Spectrum:  
1. **Kenotic theory** (original): emptied of divinity/form/equality → exchange form of God for servant. Objections Hansen accepts: no second object needed beyond *himself*; adversative *but* separates from form of God; defined by participles *taking/becoming* — emptying “not by subtracting from but by adding to”; metaphorical/poetic. Original kenotic theory “discredited.” Modified kenosis (Lightfoot, Martin): divest glories/prerogatives/station, not divine nature — reaction against kenosis goes too far if it says hymn gives “no clue” what emptied of; contrast form of God / form of slave is a clue.  
2. **Incarnation view:** emptying = incarnation as slave; form of slave = opposite of glory (lowest position, powerless, no rights, shame); slavery as extreme deprivation of rights; gave up **appearance** of divinity while still existing in form of God; O’Brien: displayed nature of God in form of slave; Calvin/Barth: divinity concealed/incognito. TNIV “made himself nothing”; Pauline uses of empty = make powerless (1 Cor 1:17; Rom 4:14).  
3. **Servant of the Lord (Isa 53:12):** *emptied himself* echoes “poured out his life to death”; other Isa links (52:13–14; 53:3–4, 12; and Phil 2:10–11 quotes Isa 45:23). Jeremias: emptying = death not incarnation — Hansen: chronological structure of hymn (preincarnate choice → incarnation → humiliation → cross) makes emptying-as-cross hard; allusion enriches without full chronological identity — emptying is incarnation **leading to** death. Honor-of-Servant vs humiliation-of-slave objection underplays Isa 53 graphic humiliation.  
- **Hansen’s synthesis:** “Christ did not empty himself of his divinity… but he did surrender his divine rights and cloaked his divine glory by becoming human in the form of a slave. His existence in the form of God was both manifested and concealed… His act of self-emptying was the incarnation; the result… humiliation, suffering, and death… Like the Suffering Servant… ‘poured out his soul unto death.’”  
- Locus: D ll. 95–119

**C13. Taking form of slave / becoming human likeness.**  
Taking + becoming simultaneous means of self-emptying. Slave = mission, not class: “without advantage… completely at the service of all”; not to be served but to serve (John 13:3–5 illustration, whether or not hymn reflects that tradition). *Becoming* (aorist) vs *existing* (present): entry into new state / “being born” sense (John 8:58; Rom 1:3; Gal 4:4). *Likeness*: neither total identity with fallen humanity (sin, loss of divine form) nor mere facade/docetic mask; ambiguity guards mystery — full humanity + retained equality with God and sinless obedience. *Anthropoi* = human beings, not male-only.  
- Locus: D ll. 121–127

**C14. “Found in appearance as a human being.”**  
Empirical discovery of genuine humanity; progressive synthetic parallelism; *and* introduces new sentence modifying **he humbled himself** (not the emptying). Second downward step: as examined human being, same person “takes in that capacity the same step into the depths once again” (Barth). Confirms decision not to exploit advantageous position.  
- Locus: D ll. 130–135

**C15. Humbled himself; Isa 53 echo with differences; ethical link to 2:1–5.**  
Possible echo of Isa 53:8 LXX “in humiliation”; differences: Isa “my servant” = honor vs hymn slave = no rights; Isa passive lamb vs hymn active self-humbling/obedience; Isa 53:12 pour out ≠ Phil emptying (incarnation) + unto death (cross) as separate events. Still: clear parallel of humiliation identifies Jesus with Suffering Servant. Embodies Prov 15:33/22:4; Matt 23:12 etc.; Jas 4:10; 1 Pet 5:6. **Immediate context:** “Christ humbled himself” = explicit connection to “in humility value others above yourselves” (2:3). Exemplar not step-by-step copy of unique incarnation/crucifixion/exaltation/universal worship; yet ethical parallel: church humility grounded in Christ’s self-humbling obedience.  
- Locus: D ll. 137–143

**C16. Obedience unto death; object of obedience; interests of others.**  
Humiliation voluntary; *unto death* = degree not duration (“nth degree”). Object not specified in hymn; inferred God (from God exalted him; glory of Father) and, via 2:4 context, service of others / “ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Application 2:12: community obedience to God in service to each other.  
- Locus: D ll. 143–145

**C17. “Even death on a cross” — climax, shame, paradox.**  
Shameful not heroic death; Roman law for worst criminals/slaves/foreigners not citizens; Cicero quotes; for Philippi as Roman colony drives home lowest rung. Greatest contrast: form of God … death on a cross. Cross instrument of self-emptying and self-humbling; ultimate fulfillment of divine intention of one equal to God.  
- Locus: D ll. 147–151

**C18. “Death on a cross” integral vs Pauline addition (authorship-of-line debate).**  
**Position many interpreters:** words break metrical symmetry + reflect Pauline theology → Pauline addition.  
**Hansen’s position:** integral to original hymn before Paul used it; “climax to which the last three verses have been pointing.” Cross in hymn not Paul’s usual “for us” redemptive formula (Gal 2:20; 3:13; 6:14) — centered exclusively on Christ’s decisive self-emptying/humbling; benefits “for us” may be inferred from surrounding context only. Paradox: celebrates slave-death as achievement of one existing in form of God — down to “deepest, darkest hellhole,” not creation hymns (Ps 19; John 1:3; Col 1:16).  
- Locus: D ll. 152–155

---

### B. 2:9–11 — Exaltation / name / Isa 45 / imperial cult / monotheism

**C19. Structure of second sentence.**  
First sentence ends lowest place (cross); second begins total reversal: “Therefore also God highly exalted him.” Christ remains central: subject of self-humiliation; object of God’s exaltation/universal worship.  
- Locus: D ll. 165

**C20. “Therefore also” and reward debate.**  
*Therefore* inferential: self-humbling reason for exaltation/name; *also* marks reciprocity (himself/him).  
**Strong No to reward:**  
- Calvin: avoid profane speculation of meriting divine honors; conjunction = consequence not reason.  
- Barth: not sequence/reward but identity of abased one with Exalted Lord.  
- Hawthorne: natural/logical outcome of humility; inflexible kingdom law (self-humbling → exaltation).  
**Hansen’s assessment:** insights correct flawed quid pro quo; *gave* (*charizomai*) = free grace defines exaltation; yet Calvin’s redefinition “extremely doubtful”; Barth denies narrative sequence; Hawthorne too impersonal.  
**Hansen’s Yes, qualified:** exaltation as personal reward for obedience, **with four qualifications**: (1) reward not motive of obedience; (2) not redemption-from-sin earned by obedience; (3) gracious gift / proof of divine approval not compensation; (4) confirmation of true identity (form of God / equality) hidden by cross, revealed by exaltation/name Lord — not acquisition of new position.  
- Locus: D ll. 167–173

**C21. *Hyperypsōsen* = superlative highest place, not higher than preincarnate.**  
Unique NT compound; TNIV “to the highest place”; not comparative elevation above pre-incarnate status; confirmed by name *above* every name and every knee three spheres. Ps 97:9 LXX *hyperypsōsen* of Yahweh: incomparable class, not one step above other gods (O’Brien).  
- Locus: D ll. 175

**C22. Name given = Lord, not Jesus.**  
Exalted defined by *gave* the name above every name.  
**Moule (reported):** name = Jesus, made highest by God-like self-giving; support from “in the name of Jesus.”  
**Hansen/majority:** name given at exaltation = **Lord**; Jesus named at incarnation; divine title postponed to final acclamation “Jesus Christ is Lord”; Isa 41–45 uniqueness of LORD/Yahweh; quoting Isa 45:23 appropriates unique divine name for Jesus. Parabolic shape: form of God → form of slave → name Lord.  
- Locus: D ll. 177–187

**C23. Imperial cult / Caesar resonance at Philippi.**  
In Roman colony, acclamation Jesus is Lord heard as “shocking allusion” to imperial cult “Caesar is Lord.” Imperial ideology: Jupiter/gods gave divine authority/names to Augustus; hymn theology: God gave divine name to Jesus for universal acclamation. Paul presents exaltation “in language that reflects and subverts the Roman imperial cult.”  
- Locus: D ll. 189

**C24. “In the name of Jesus” = worship of Jesus as Lord.**  
Not merely occasion (“when name mentioned”) or means (Jesus as mediator of worship to God). Phrase links back to name given and forward to acclamation; ties humiliation half (human named Jesus, slave, cross) to exaltation half. Inserts “in the name of Jesus” where Isa 45:23 has “before me” — Jesus bears name of God; worship as Lord to glory of Father; “directly and uniquely associated with God.”  
- Locus: D ll. 191–193

**C25. Every knee — three spheres; not glad universalism.**  
Bowing = supplication, abasement, worship, subjection; church anticipates all creation. Heaven / earth / under earth: ancient cosmology of spirit-powers; all angels, demons, humans, creation under Lord Jesus. *Acknowledge* = open declaration, not necessarily glad praise; Isa 45:24 includes those who raged and are put to shame; not universal church but every creature’s irrevocable admission of rightful Lordship; church worship previews that acknowledgment.  
- Locus: D ll. 195–199

**C26. Climactic revelation of name “Lord” — three dimensions.**  
Dramatic withholding until universal voice. Dimensions:  
1. **Sovereignty:** Bauckham on Jewish monotheism — universal sovereignty intrinsic to unique divine identity, not delegable; Decalogue forbids bowing to heavenly/earthly/under-earth things; God gives Jesus divine sovereignty.  
2. **Identity:** Not Hellenistic polytheistic enthronement of a deity (despite descent-ascent myth parallels some claim); Jewish monotheism via Isa 45. *Kyrios* = LXX substitute (~6,156×) for YHWH; name above every name = YHWH’s unique name given to Jesus; not one Hellenistic lord or mere rival of Caesar.  
3. **Destiny / already–not yet:** God already gave name; universal acknowledgment still future; eschatological structure; church under suffering sings vindication; “earthly center from which the full Lordship of Christ becomes visible”; Jesus on cross not Caesar on throne destined for universal acknowledgment.  
- Locus: D ll. 201–207

**C27. Final line: glory of God the Father; christological monotheism.**  
Whole hymn summarized: self-emptying not for glory apart from God; self-giving of Jesus expresses nature of God — “The one true God consists, through and through, of self-giving love”; Lordship of Jesus expresses God as Creator-Ruler. Mystery of unity unexplained; Shema maintained in revised form: one God = Lord Jesus Christ and God the Father → “new **christological monotheism**”; full equality (2:6) + unique name Lord (2:9–11) without division; reverence to Jesus = “extension of the worship of God.” Full circle form of God → glory of Father; “The meaning of the word ‘God’ includes not only Jesus, but specifically, the crucified Jesus.”  
- Locus: D ll. 209–213

---

### C. Connection hymn → community (restated in 2:12–18 intro)

**C28. After hymn, paraenesis resumes gospel-worthy living.**  
Returns to practical guidelines; continues 1:27 manner worthy of gospel; hymn strengthens unity appeals (1:27; 2:2) and founds “work out your salvation… without grumbling or arguing” (2:12, 14). True worship inspires work; Christ “unifying center.” Bonhoeffer quote on community through Christ.  
- Locus: D ll. 215–219

**C29. “Therefore” = intended results of hymn.**  
Cross, exaltation, universal worship not abstract; lead to reconciliation among those who confess Jesus is Lord.  
- Locus: D ll. 221

---

### D. 2:12–18 — Work out salvation / lights / drink offering

**C30. First application = obedience.**  
Picks up hymn: Christ “obedient to death.” “My dear friends” / “my beloved” — friendship theme (1:8; 4:1). “Always obeyed… much more in my absence” — memory of gospel acceptance (4:15) and partnership (1:5). Obedience = conformity to gospel; already obeying gospel-in-hymn by following Christ’s obedience and acknowledging Lordship; relational not legal (knowing/being like/serving Christ). Christ Lord of all; Paul mere servant (1:1), desires eclipse by Christ (1:21).  
- Locus: D ll. 223–225

**C31. “Continue to work out your salvation.”**  
TNIV “continue” supplies elliptical force. *Work out* = bring about, produce, create (Rom 4:15; 5:3; 7:8; 2 Cor 4:17). Surprise vs Paul’s grace/faith salvation (1:28; Rom 4:5; 10:10; 1 Thess 5:9).  
- Locus: D ll. 227–231

**C32. Corporate/ecclesiological sense of the imperative.**  
Context = social harmony: 1:27; 2:2; 2:14. Command “in a corporate sense”: whole church (spiritually ill 2:3–4) restore health/integrity/wholeness. Plural verb/pronoun; not merely individualistic eternal salvation. Still each individual’s responsibility.  
- Locus: D ll. 233–235

**C33. “Salvation” not redefined as mere social health.**  
Some: *sōtēria* = corporate well-being (Greek civic prayers; Plato; Mark/Acts health). Hansen: good evidence for social concern, but redefinition inadequate vs Paul’s customary **future eschatological** use (1:28; 3:20–21); frame between 2:9–10 universal confession and 2:16 day of Christ. Prefer: “present outworking of their eschatological salvation within the believing community” — colony of heaven (3:20) made earthly experience by working out promised salvation; implements 2:4 interests of others.  
- Locus: D ll. 237–241

**C34. Presence/absence not euphemism for death.**  
Not impending departure; Paul confident of soon visit (2:24). Friendship presence-absence language; letter as presence for unity in absence. Work out salvation **much more** in absence — independence of Paul.  
- Locus: D ll. 243–245

**C35. “With fear and trembling.”**  
OT: awe before God / fear of Israel due to God (Exod 15:16; Deut 2:25 etc.). Paul: 1 Cor 2:3; 2 Cor 7:15; Eph 6:5.  
**Some interpreters:** humility/respect **toward one another** (fits 2:3; 2:14).  
**Hansen more likely:** attitude in **presence of God** — after 2:9–11 worship scene and before 2:13 God who works; fear of Lord dispels selfish ambition/vain conceit (2:3). Jewish union of fear with love (Deut 10:12); Paul 2 Cor 5:11, 14; paradox with “fear not” / perfect love casts out fear.  
- Locus: D ll. 247–249

**C36. 2:13 — God works in you to will and to act for his good purpose.**  
Reason for confidence amid community-shredding ambition. God initiated, sustains, will complete; *energeō* = put capabilities into operation. Not passivism (“let go and let God”) nor residual activism (“God helps those who help themselves”); absolute necessity of empowering presence for work **and desire**. *In you* = individuals and community. God-driven purpose; originator of willing and working. Same verb for God’s work and ours; Infinite Worker; God’s indicative enables human imperative; Ps 127:1.  
- Locus: D ll. 251–259

**C37. “Good purpose” = God’s, not human goodwill.**  
Some (social harmony emphasis): human goodwill toward one another (no *his* in Greek). Hansen: article with abstract noun reflexive → God; noun usually divine benevolent purpose (Hawthorne admits); tautology if human will again; majority: God’s good will; goal fulfilled when Christians live in harmony.  
- Locus: D ll. 261

**C38. 2:14 — Do everything without grumbling or arguing.**  
Long sentence 2:14–16. Everything = all life under salvation (1 Cor 10:31; Col 3:17). Grumbling = secret complaints/backbiting; arguing = divisive quarreling. Echo Israel wilderness (Num 14; Exod 16; Num 17; 1 Cor 10:10 warning). Object of Philippians’ grumbling not stated — Hansen **speculates** (not asserts) from clues: suffering (1:29); leaders (unity calls; Epaphroditus 2:29; Euodia/Syntyche 4:2; overseers/deacons 1:1); possibly Paul (1:12–17; 2:2, 14–16). Sure point: serious threat to unity. Fulfillment of working out salvation visible when life without grumbling/arguing; “essential evidence of salvation” = deliverance from those habits.  
- Locus: D ll. 263–269

**C39. 2:15 — Blameless, pure, without fault children of God.**  
Purpose: become *amemptoi*, *akeraioi*, *amoma* — corporate speech ethics, not isolationist moralism. Children of God = Spirit adoption (Gal 3–4; Rom 8); express who they already are by grace (2:13). Contrast “warped and crooked generation.”  
- Locus: D ll. 271–273

**C40. Deut 32:5 LXX twist — not church-replacement of Israel.**  
Deut 32:5: degenerate children = perverse generation; Paul: unblemished children **in** warped generation. Some: church takes Israel’s place (cf. Phil 3:3 circumcision claim). Hansen: ironic echo contrasts church/Israel as negative example but “does not provide foundation” for replacement; Gentile church grafted; all Israel will be saved (Rom 11); irrevocable gifts. Main point: contrast children of God vs world.  
- Locus: D ll. 273–275

**C41. Shine like stars in the world.**  
Hansen’s trans: “among whom you shine like stars in the world”; heavenly bodies. Echo Dan 12:3 LXX; Paul shifts “stars of heaven” → “in the world” = worldwide mission; Philippi community light for lost generation. Middle/passive *shine*: appear or shine — same effect. Form could be imperative; location in dependent clause → **indicative** “you are shining” (vision motivating 2:14); parallel Matt 5:14–16 indicative→imperative.  
- Locus: D ll. 277

**C42. Hold firmly the word of life.**  
How become blameless shining children. Verb: grasp/maintain; primarily **defensive** posture amid opposition (1:27–28), yielding evangelistic results; some stress evangelistic “holding forth.” *Word of life* ≈ gospel synonym; **immediate reference = Christ hymn** (2:5–11); living worthy of gospel (1:27). Loss of word → black hole not star.  
- Locus: D ll. 279–283

**C43. Boast on the day of Christ; run/labor not in vain.**  
Personal incentive: Paul will boast if quality of their life shows ministry not vain. *Boast* seems odd after humility/cross/glory of Father; fits Paul’s inverted boasting theme (in Lord, cross, weakness; about converts by God’s grace 2:13). Day of Christ / judgment seat (2 Cor 5:10 etc.); runner/laborer self-portraits; confidence in God completing work (1:6) still urges evidence.  
- Locus: D ll. 283–287

**C44. 2:17 Drink offering on their sacrifice and service.**  
Progression from run/labor to ultimate sacrifice metaphor. Even if poured out, glad and rejoice with them. Jewish + Greek libation imagery; LXX drink offerings (Num 28:7); Gentile readers understand.  
**Debate: ministry sufferings vs martyrdom.**  
- Against martyrdom: present tense; verb not = blood-shedding; 2:24 visit confidence; trio of ministry metaphors; joy + martyrdom unlikely.  
- Hansen: still **possibility** of martyrdom (“even if”); concessive not forecast; 2 Tim 4:6 parallel for metaphor of death; no contradiction with 2:24; metaphorical sacrificial language; resemblance to Christ emptied himself (2:7) — poured out unto death like Christ; joy in solidarity with Christ and with Philippians’ sacrifice.  
**Sacrifice and service:** Calvin (via Rom 15:16): Paul offers Philippians as priest. **Majority/Hansen:** both nouns = Philippians’ sacrifice/service (one article; 2:30; 4:18); Paul’s libation **addition to / completion of** theirs (*on* ≈ in addition to). TNIV “coming from your faith.” Concrete: Epaphroditus gifts = fragrant offering (4:17–18); partnership in gospel (1:5); priestly status elevated.  
- Locus: D ll. 289–303

**C45. 2:18 Mutual joy in partnership.**  
They should be glad and rejoice with him; not depressed by his imprisonment. Not masochism; basis = partnership in gospel (1:5), Spirit (2:1), sufferings of Christ (3:10). *With* prefix → partnership theme. Section arc: negative (no grumbling) → positive (rejoice with me); joy distinguishing mark of partners in Christ even in suffering/sacrifice/service.  
- Locus: D ll. 305–307

## Key structural points

1. **Hymn narrative arc (as Hansen reads in D):** preincarnate equality/glory → refusal to exploit → self-emptying incarnation as slave → genuine humanity → active self-humbling obedience → death on a cross → **therefore also** God hyper-exalts → gifts name Lord → universal knee/tongue → glory of Father.  
2. **Two sentences:** (A) Christ’s downward actions to cross; (B) God’s upward actions to universal worship; Christ central throughout.  
3. **Ethical frame (restated):** 2:1–5 humility/interests of others; hymn as perfect exemplar (not copyable script); 2:12–18 obedience, corporate outworking of eschatological salvation, speech ethics, mission as stars, partnership joy.  
4. **Theological load-bearing moves Hansen owns:** preexistence from narrative sequence; *morphē* via glory; *harpagmos* as non-exploitation of possessed equality; kenosis as incarnation (cloak glory, not lose deity); exaltation as gracious vindication/revelation not promotion into deity; name = YHWH/*kyrios*; christological monotheism; Isa 45 application; imperial cult subversion at Philippi.  
5. **2:12–18 structure:** therefore → obedience → work out salvation (corporate eschatological) with fear/trembling → God works → no grumbling → blameless children vs crooked generation → shine as stars → hold word of life → Paul’s boast day of Christ → drink offering joy → mutual rejoice.
